940.specification: This module is a TLC support module for model checking the specification of LiveInternalMemory. It provides concrete replacements for the constant operators Send, Reply, and InitMemInt so that TLC can evaluate transitions involving the internal memory interface, and it also defines a liveness formula requiring every processor to be busy infinitely often. In addition, it defines a large PostCondition value describing a specific counterexample trace as a structured record containing action and state snapshots.

941.specification: This module is a TLC model-checking wrapper for the write-through cache specification from LiveWriteThroughCache. It manually instantiates definitions corresponding to the internal-memory liveness specification, using a refinement mapping from the cache implementation state variables to abstract memory variables omem, octl, and obuf, because the comments explain that the TLC version targeted here cannot handle the intended INSTANCE-based instantiation directly. The file defines initial-state, next-state, type-invariant, enabledness, liveness, and combined specification formulas for the instantiated internal memory view, and also includes constants and a PostCondition value describing a counterexample-shaped structure for model checking.

942.specification: This module provides a TLAPS proof of a theorem about the HourClock specification, specifically that the invariant HCini is preserved by the HourClock system. The proof shows that if HC holds, then HCini holds always, by proving that HCini is preserved by the next-state relation HCnxt. The proof is structured hierarchically and uses the PTL backend for temporal logic reasoning.

943.specification: This specification models a simple 12-hour clock. The state variable 'hr' represents the current hour, which ranges from 1 to 12. The initial predicate HCini ensures that hr starts within this range. The next-state action HCnxt increments hr by 1 unless it is 12, in which case it wraps around to 1. The temporal property HC asserts that the system starts in a valid state and always evolves according to HCnxt. The theorem proves that the invariant HCini is always maintained. The design is straightforward, with no fault model or concurrency, and focuses on demonstrating a cyclic counter with a simple temporal invariant.

944.specification: This module provides a TLAPS proof for the InternalMemory specification, specifically proving that the type invariant (TypeInvariant) is preserved by the system. The proof addresses the fact that TypeInvariant alone is not inductive due to the way the next-state action Do(p) accesses fields of buf[p], which are only valid when buf[p] is in MReq. To resolve this, the invariant is strengthened with BufConsistent, which ensures that buf[p] has the correct type depending on the value of ctl[p]. The main theorem proved is that ISpec implies []TypeInvariant, using the strengthened invariant Inv (TypeInvariant /\ BufConsistent). The proof is structured hierarchically and uses TLAPS proof commands and backend solvers.

945.specification: This module specifies an internal memory system that implements the MemoryInterface. The system models a set of processes interacting with a shared memory, where each process can issue memory requests, perform operations, and receive responses. The state is tracked by variables for memory contents (mem), control state per process (ctl), and per-process buffers (buf). The algorithm models request, operation, and response phases for each process, with explicit state transitions and primed variables. The specification asserts a type invariant is always maintained, and the main temporal property (ISpec) requires that the system starts in a valid initial state and all steps follow the allowed transitions, with the type invariant holding globally. The design uses explicit state transitions and does not model faults or failures.

946.specification: This module specifies a real-time refinement of an hour clock by adding a real-time variable now and an auxiliary timer variable t. It constrains elapsed time between hour-clock ticks HCnxt so that each tick occurs within a tolerance window determined by SecondsPerHour and Rho, and it also states progress/fairness properties ensuring time can continue to advance. The specification includes state predicates and temporal formulas for timer behavior, upper and lower timing bounds, non-Zeno progress, recurrence of every hour value, and an error temporal property about now remaining different from 4.

947.specification: This module specifies a simple real-time framework with a single clock variable now ranging over a bounded set of natural-number time values from 0 to MaxReal. It defines an initialization predicate for time, a real-time next-state relation RTNext(v) that either advances time while keeping an auxiliary state component v unchanged or keeps time fixed while allowing v to change, and a timer transition rule TimerNext that updates a timer variable t based on whether an action A occurs or is disabled. The specification also defines a fairness condition RTFairness(v) requiring weak fairness of time-progress steps above every real threshold, but it does not define a complete top-level Spec operator in this file.

948.specification: This specification defines a real-time memory-related wrapper around an internal memory specification. The top-level module introduces a positive real-time bound constant Rho, defines an inner module in which a response action forces a process control state to become "rdy", and requires that every process satisfy a real-time bound RTBound on that response action together with the imported internal-memory specification ISpec. The top-level property RTSpec existentially quantifies the internal state variables mem, ctl, and buf and states that there exists an instance of the inner real-time internal-memory specification satisfying RTISpec; the file uses imported real-time operators but does not itself define transition-system variables or proofs.

949.specification: This module defines a real-time wrapper around an existing write-through cache specification. It extends the underlying cache model with an additional variable lastP and a scheduling discipline that uses a computed position order to control which process may take certain expensive actions, specifically read misses and writes, while preserving other cache and memory queue actions. The specification assumes real-time parameters Delta, Epsilon, and Rho are positive reals satisfying a timing bound, and it asserts a real-time temporal specification RTSpec that combines initialization, a next-state relation, bounded-response timing constraints via RTBound, and the RTnow clocking condition; it finally states a theorem that this real-time specification implies the instantiated RTMemory real-time specification.

950.specification: This specification models a real-time hour clock by combining a real-valued time variable with an underlying hour-clock module. The outer module introduces a continuously increasing real-valued variable now and assumes a positive timing tolerance constant Rho; an inner module defines a timer variable t that is reset when the underlying hour clock advances and otherwise accumulates elapsed real time. The specification asserts timing bounds showing that the hour clock advances no later than 3600 + Rho seconds and, when it advances, no earlier than 3600 - Rho seconds, and the top-level behavior combines the inherited hour-clock behavior, monotonic real time, and the existence of an inner timer instance satisfying these real-time constraints.

951.specification: This module defines real-time temporal constraints over actions by introducing an explicit real-valued time variable `now` and auxiliary timer behavior. The operator `RTBound(A, v, D, E)` specifies that there exists a timer `t` which is reset when action `A` occurs or when `A` becomes disabled in the next state, otherwise advances by the elapsed real time `now' - now`, while also enforcing an upper bound `E` and a lower bound `D` relative to occurrences of `A`. The operator `RTnow(v)` constrains `now` to range over the reals, to increase monotonically through a stuttering-insensitive next-state action `NowNext`, and adds a weak fairness condition ensuring time can always progress past any real threshold.

952.specification: This module is a small TLA+ example that uses ASSUME statements to have TLC check the truth of simple mathematical and logical formulas. It models no stateful algorithm and introduces no variables; instead, it evaluates propositional logic and elementary set-theoretic identities over constants a through g, booleans, and finite sets. The file demonstrates bounded quantification, logical equivalences, and basic set operators, and defines a helper operator SomeSets as the powerset of {a, b, c, d, e}.

953.specification: This module defines a standard TLA+ representation of bags (multisets) as functions from elements to positive natural numbers, where the domain contains exactly the elements present in the bag and the function value gives the multiplicity. It provides operators for recognizing bags, converting between sets and bags, bag membership, empty bags, bag union and difference, subbag comparison, the set of all subbags, image construction over bags, cardinality, and counting copies of an element. The module is a pure mathematical library module rather than a transition-system specification: it has no variables, actions, or temporal properties, and its comments note that most operators are overridden by TLC except for SubBag.

954.specification: This module defines the standard finite-set operators `IsFiniteSet` and `Cardinality`. It characterizes finiteness by the existence of a finite sequence whose elements cover the set, and it defines cardinality recursively over subsets by removing one chosen element at a time until the empty set is reached. The file contains no state variables, no actions, and no temporal specification; it is a pure mathematical utility module with comments explaining that TLC overrides these operators in Java.

955.specification: This module is a dummy replacement for the standard TLA+ Integers module. It extends Naturals and provides placeholder definitions for integer-related operators, with comments explaining that tools such as TLC are expected to override these definitions with real implementations. The module defines the integer set Int as the empty set and defines the prefix negation operator in terms of subtraction, serving as a structural specification stub rather than a complete algorithmic system.

956.specification: This module is a dummy placeholder specification for the standard Naturals module rather than an algorithm or distributed system. It defines placeholder versions of natural-number-related operators such as arithmetic, comparisons, and ranges, with comments explaining that real tools are expected to override them with proper implementations. The file contains no state variables, no transition system, no temporal behavior, no fault model, and no verified safety or liveness properties; its notable design decision is that most operators are given trivial or symbolic definitions solely as stand-ins.

957.specification: This module axiomatizes the Peano natural numbers using three parameters: a carrier set N, a distinguished zero element Z, and a successor function Sc. The main operator PeanoAxioms states that zero is in N, successor maps N to N, every non-zero element is the successor of some element, and every subset of N containing zero and closed under successor is all of N. The module then assumes existence of such a structure and defines Succ, Nat, and Zero by CHOOSE expressions to extract a particular successor function, its domain as the naturals, and a corresponding zero element.

958.specification: This module axiomatizes and then selects a model of the real numbers on top of a Peano-style natural-number foundation imported from the Peano module. It defines a predicate IsModelOfReals(R, Plus, Times, Leq) expressing algebraic, order, and completeness properties of a real-number structure, proves existentially that some such model exists, then chooses one witness RM and introduces derived operators for Real numbers, infinities, arithmetic, ordering, subtraction, division, integers, and exponentiation. The specification is not a transition-system or fault-tolerant protocol model; instead it is a mathematical TLA+ theory module with no variables, no actions, and no temporal behavior, focused on abstract construction and characterization of reals and extended-real-like values.

959.specification: This module provides placeholder definitions for real-number-related operators rather than a full executable semantics. It models a dummy Reals module by defining a distinguished value Real, division as a CHOOSE-based operator over that value, and Infinity as a CHOOSE of an element outside Real that is greater than every element of Real. The file does not define a transition system, state variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness, or proofs; it is a mathematical support module intended for use by other specifications and tools.

960.specification: This module defines standard operators for finite sequences in TLA+, representing a sequence of length n as a function with domain 1..n. It provides constructors and selectors such as Seq, Len, concatenation, Append, Head, Tail, SubSeq, and SelectSeq, with comments explaining their intended meaning and the representation of tuples as sequences. The module is a library-style definitions module rather than a transition-system specification: it declares no variables, no actions, and no temporal properties, and it notes that TLC overrides these operators with Java implementations.

961.specification: This module defines a grammar for the TLA+ language itself using grammar-combinator style operators imported from other modules. It defines lexical classes, operator-token classes, and a parameterized grammar operator P inside TLAPlusGrammar, then returns LeastGrammar(P). It is not a state-machine specification and contains no variables, actions, or temporal correctness properties.

962.specification: This module specifies the correctness skeleton of the alternating-bit protocol using sender and receiver bit variables together with sent and received data values. The sender may send a new value when its acknowledgement bit matches its send bit, the receiver may accept a message when its receive bit differs from the sender bit, and the sender may accept an acknowledgement when the receiver bit differs from the sender acknowledgement bit. The specification defines an initial condition, a next-state relation, a type invariant, fairness assumptions for message reception and acknowledgement reception, and a temporal property stating that the sender and acknowledgement bits are infinitely often out of sync.

963.specification: This module provides a TLAPS proof of type correctness for the Alternating Bit protocol, as specified in AlternatingBit.tla. The main theorem proved is that the specification ABSpec implies that the type invariant ABTypeInv always holds. The proof is structured hierarchically, with supporting lemmas establishing the type preservation of sequence operations such as Append, Tail, and Head, as well as the correctness of the Lose operation. The proof uses standard TLAPS commands and relies on the AlternatingBit and TLAPS modules for definitions and proof infrastructure.

964.specification: This module specifies the alternating bit protocol as a simple sender-receiver communication system with separate message and acknowledgment queues. The sender keeps a data value and a control bit, retransmits when an acknowledgment has not yet matched the current bit, and the receiver records the last received bit and data value while sending acknowledgments back. The environment may nondeterministically lose one element from either queue, and the specification checks a type invariant over the protocol state under a temporal specification with weak fairness for retransmission and acknowledgment sending and strong fairness for message and acknowledgment receipt.

965.specification: This module defines a grammar for TLA+ configuration files using operators from the BNFGrammars module. It characterizes lexical classes such as letters, digits, identifiers, keywords, strings, and numbers, and then builds a grammar for configuration statements like SPECIFICATION, INIT, NEXT, VIEW, SYMMETRY, constraints, properties, constant replacements, and constant assignments. The specification is purely structural and declarative: it introduces no state variables, no transition actions, and no temporal correctness properties, but instead defines the accepted syntax of config files via grammar combinators and a LET-local grammar parameterized operator.

966.specification: This module is a model-checking harness around an alternating-bit protocol specification imported from another module. It adds queue-length constraints, states liveness and temporal properties about sent data eventually being received and about possible permanent disagreement of protocol bits, and records a concrete postcondition/counterexample structure using TLC-style trace data. The file also introduces a derived action-temporal formula and a simple stability property over sent data, while composing a combined specification from the imported protocol specification and an added temporal condition.

967.specification: This module models the classic balance-scale stone-cutting problem: given a total weight W and N pieces, find an ordered partition of W into N natural-number weights such that every target weight from 1 to W can be balanced using those pieces on either side of the scale. The specification encodes weighing by allowing coefficients in {-1, 0, 1}, where a negative coefficient represents placing a piece on the same side as the object being weighed. It uses recursive operators to enumerate ordered partitions and to sum sequences, and then uses TLC-oriented ASSUME formulas with PrintT to search for and display a solution or report that no solution exists.

968.specification: This specification models a state-graph exploration algorithm that searches a directed graph represented as a record with components `states`, `initials`, and `actions`. The explorer does not enforce BFS ordering: the frontier `S` is a set, and the next state to explore is chosen non-deterministically, while it still records predecessor edges and level information to reconstruct a counterexample path. It checks for safety violations and deadlocks, reconstructs a path once termination is detected, and asserts temporal properties for overall termination and for eventual discovery of a violation state together with a valid counterexample path, under weak fairness of `Next`.

969.specification: This module defines a collection of directed state graphs together with associated violation sets and example counterexample paths, intended for testing model-checker specifications such as TLCMC and MCReachability. Each graph is represented as a record with fields for the set of states, the set of initial states, and a sequence of successor-state sets indexed by state number; separate operators define the corresponding violating states and witness traces. The module contains no variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness, or proofs; instead it serves as a static data library that selects one named test case based on the IO environment variable GRAPH, defaulting to graph 7 when that setting is absent.

970.specification: This module models a TLC-like reachability model checker that performs breadth-first exploration over a graph of states, with a parameter K controlling whether exploration is strict BFS (K = 1) or degraded non-strict BFS (K > 1) to approximate multiple workers. The state graph is given as a record with states, initial states, and an action relation, and the model checker tracks explored states, a queue of pending states, predecessor information, and BFS levels in order to detect violations and reconstruct counterexamples. The specification verifies termination of the translated PlusCal algorithm and a liveness-style property stating that when violation states exist, the eventual counterexample belongs to a supplied set of known counterexamples, with an additional minimal-length requirement when K = 1; it also includes a refinement mapping to an instantiated MCReachability specification.

971.specification: This module is a small test harness for TLCMC that uses graphs defined externally through an instance substitution into the TLCMC module. It declares several variables and a worker-count helper operator, then instantiates TLCMC with a state graph, violation states, a worker count K, a trivial constraint given by a lambda that always returns TRUE, and counterexamples, all supplied through names from other modules or environments. The file itself does not define an algorithmic transition system, actions, or temporal correctness properties; instead, it wires together an instantiated model-checking setup for testing graphs.

972.specification: This module is a small test harness for model-checking reachability over a state graph. It uses graphs defined externally in the StateGraphs module and instantiates another module, MCReachability, by supplying a state graph and a set of violation states from TestCase. The file itself contains no algorithm steps, no state-transition actions, and no temporal properties; it primarily declares variables and provides an INSTANCE substitution setup for the reachability checker.

973.specification: This module provides wrapper theorems that expose TypeOK and Inv as named invariants of the Spec for the SimpleRegular algorithm. The actual inductive content and algorithmic details are contained in the imported SimpleRegular module; this file focuses on stating and proving that TypeOK and Inv are invariants under the system's specification. The proofs are structured hierarchically and use TLAPS proof constructs, but do not introduce new algorithmic content or state variables. The design is intended for proof management and clarity, making the invariants explicit for use in further verification or as proof obligations.

974.specification: This module specifies an N-process shared-memory algorithm in which each process writes its own shared register and then reads a neighbor's register, using regular registers rather than atomic registers for the shared x values. The model represents a regular register by a set of possible values, so a write from 0 to 1 is modeled by first changing a register value from {0} to {0,1} and then to {1}; a read may return any element currently in that set. The specification defines the translated PlusCal actions, an initial condition, the next-state relation, a termination condition, a safety property PCorrect stating that if all processes are done then some y[i] equals 1, an inductive invariant Inv used to prove that property, and two TLAPS proofs establishing correctness.

975.specification: This module provides wrapper theorems that expose TypeOK and Inv as named invariants of the Spec specification. The actual inductive content and system model are defined in the imported Simple module, specifically in its Correctness property. The theorems here formally state that Spec implies the invariance of TypeOK and Inv, and provide structured proofs using TLAPS proof steps. No algorithm or system is directly modeled in this file; instead, it serves as a proof harness for properties defined elsewhere.

976.specification: This module specifies a simple concurrent ring algorithm with N processes arranged in a circle. Each process first sets its own x entry to 1, then copies the left neighbor's x value into its own y entry; the specification includes the PlusCal algorithm in comments and its translated TLA+ form with variables x, y, and pc. The model assumes N is a positive natural number, defines the behavior with Init, Next, and Spec, asserts termination as eventual completion of all processes, and proves a safety property stating that when all processes are done, at least one process has y[i] = 1. The file also develops an inductive invariant Inv, includes type correctness constraints, and contains TLAPS proofs of the main correctness theorem in two versions.

977.specification: This module defines several equivalent TLA+ formulations of the transitive closure of a binary relation represented as a set of ordered pairs. It develops multiple definitions: one based on paths as sequences, one using bounded sequences for finite relations, one using iterative relational composition, one recursive closure formulation, one Warshall-style recursive algorithm, and one formulation for relations represented as Boolean-valued operators over a set. The module uses assumptions to check, on small finite instances, that these different definitions are equivalent; it does not model a concurrent system or fault model, but rather specifies and compares mathematical definitions and their TLC-evaluable variants.

978.specification: This module specifies a simple alternating system with two state variables, v and x. The variable v acts as a control bit that alternates between 0 and 1, and each transition corresponds to one of two abstract actions: an A_0 action when v changes from 0 to 1, and an A_1 action when v changes from 1 to 0. The details of x's initial value and transition behavior are abstracted by the operator-valued constants XInit and XAct, and the temporal property Spec requires the system to start in Init and then always take Next steps.

979.specification: This module is a very small wrapper around another specification, declaring three variables p, c, and x, defining two simple helper operators, and instantiating the module TwoPhase. The operator XInit specifies an initial-state condition requiring its argument to equal 0, and XAct specifies a trivial next-state relation equating xNext with xInit. The file itself contains no temporal specification, no explicit safety or liveness theorem, and no fault model; it appears to provide parameterized initialization and action helpers for use with the instantiated module.

980.specification: This module provides a TLAPS proof that the implementation of a two-phase protocol (as specified in the TwoPhase module) refines another specification (A!Spec) under a refinement mapping. The proof focuses on the safety part of the specification, showing that the implementation maintains the invariant and that the refinement mapping preserves the required properties. The proof is structured hierarchically, with temporal and non-temporal leaf proofs, and uses backend solvers such as Z3 and PTL for certain steps. The design follows a standard approach for refinement proofs, with the temporal leaf proofs being reusable across similar specifications.

981.specification: This module specifies the two-phase handshake protocol, a fundamental hardware protocol involving a Producer and a Consumer process that alternate actions, with the Producer acting first. The protocol is modeled with variables representing the state of the Producer (p), Consumer (c), and an abstract data variable (x), with actions for each process and a temporal specification ensuring alternation. The module also demonstrates that this protocol implements the Alternate specification under a refinement mapping, using a function vBar to relate the two, and provides a detailed TLAPS proof of this implementation.

982.specification: This module is a model-checking wrapper around an instantiated YoYoNoPruning specification, using a fixed graph of nodes and edges and exposing a liveness-style postcondition over the imported state variables phase, incoming, outgoing, and mailbox. It defines a small graph directly in the module, includes a larger alternative graph in comments, and instantiates the YoYoNoPruning module without substitutions. The file does not define the algorithm's transition relation itself; instead, it records a temporal property stating that eventually all nodes remain permanently in the "down" phase, and it embeds a TLC-generated counterexample object as PostCondition showing a violating behavior trace and reachable states.

983.specification: This module is a model-checking wrapper for a Yo-Yo pruning specification. It defines a fixed graph using the operator definitions Nodes and Edges, declares the state variables active, phase, incoming, outgoing, and mailbox, and instantiates the module YoYoPruning. The file itself contains no transition relation, initialization predicate, temporal specification, assumptions, or proof content.

984.specification: This module specifies the Yo-Yo leader-election algorithm with pruning on undirected, loop-free, connected graphs over a fixed set of numbered nodes. The initial state nondeterministically chooses a connected graph over Nodes, orients each edge from the smaller endpoint to the larger one, and then models the algorithm as alternating down and up phases in which nodes exchange messages, reverse edges, prune edges, and eventually deactivate non-leader nodes. The specification includes typing and structural invariants, a liveness property stating eventual termination, and a characterization of termination as exactly the deadlock states under weak fairness of Next.

985.specification: This module specifies the Yo-Yo leader election algorithm on arbitrary strongly connected undirected graphs without self-loops, where nodes are identified by integers and the node with the smallest identifier is the eventual leader. The algorithm maintains an orientation of graph edges via incoming and outgoing neighbor sets and alternates between a down phase, where minimum identifiers are propagated toward sinks, and an up phase, where yes/no replies propagate back and edges receiving a "no" are reversed. The specification models asynchronous node steps as a state machine, assumes a strongly connected undirected input graph, and verifies type correctness, structural neighbor consistency, absence of newly created sources, and eventual stabilization to a state where only the minimum node remains the unique source and all up messages are "yes".

986.specification: This specification models the Yo-Yo leader-election algorithm on a strongly connected undirected graph, extended with pruning so that the algorithm terminates. Nodes alternate between down and up phases, exchange structured messages through mailboxes, reverse or prune edges based on replies, and eventually eliminate all but one source so that the smallest node becomes an isolated leader. The spec assumes a connected undirected graph, uses weak fairness for the main next-state action, and states both safety-style properties about graph consistency and termination-style temporal properties such as eventual termination and equivalence between deadlock and the terminated condition.

987.specification: This module models an asynchronous Byzantine consensus protocol based on Bracha, Gabriel, and Toueg's 1985 protocol, using a message-counting abstraction instead of explicit message buffers. Processes begin by proposing either 0 or 1, may become Byzantine up to a bound F, can receive ECHO and READY messages, send ECHO and READY messages when guards are satisfied, and eventually decide by moving to an accepting state. The specification includes initialization predicates for arbitrary initial proposals as well as all-0 and all-1 initial states, a weak-fairness-based temporal specification for liveness checking, type correctness, and temporal properties for validity, correctness, and agreement under the stated resilience assumption N > 3 * T with T >= F >= 0.

988.specification: This module is a TLC-oriented wrapper around an atomic commit protocol specification, extending ACP_NB and adding a few top-level properties and a concrete postcondition witness. It defines a symmetry-related permutation operator, a reformulated temporal property AC4_alt about decision stability for participants, an eventual-commit property AllMustCommit, and a large PostCondition value that encodes a specific counterexample trace and visited states. The file does not define the underlying transition system itself; instead, it refers to state imported from the extended module and packages TLC data structures for checking or replaying a counterexample scenario involving two participants p0 and p1, coordinator failure, and participant crashes.

989.specification: This module specifies an erroneous non-blocking atomic commitment protocol variant built on top of definitions imported from ACP_SB. The comments explain that the mistake is that a participant delivers a broadcast decision locally before forwarding it to other participants, which can violate the atomic commitment consistency property AC1. The module adds a forwarding field to participants, defines the corresponding type invariant and initial condition, specifies forwarding, deciding on a forwarded decision, and aborting on timeout, and then gives a temporal specification with weak fairness and a leads-to property stating that if one participant decides commit, then every participant eventually decides commit.

990.specification: This module specifies a non-blocking atomic commitment protocol variant in which reliable broadcast is used to obtain the non-blocking property. It extends a base module for atomic commitment and adds participant forwarding state so that when a participant receives a decision, it forwards that decision to all other participants before locally delivering it. The specification defines participant-side actions for forwarding, pre-deciding from forwarded or coordinator messages, deciding after forwarding is complete, and aborting on simulated timeout conditions, then combines them into a temporal specification with weak fairness assumptions and includes some invalid liveness-style properties such as all-commit, all-abort, and a yes-votes leads-to commit condition.

991.specification: This module is a TLC-oriented wrapper around the ACP_SB specification, extending the underlying protocol module and TLC. It defines a symmetry-related helper operator using permutations of the participants, and rewrites the AC4 property into an explicit stuttering-invariant temporal formula over the participant variable. It also states a liveness-style property requiring that every participant eventually reaches either the commit or abort decision state.

992.specification: This module specifies an atomic commitment protocol with one coordinator and a set of participants, using a simple broadcast mechanism in an asynchronous setting. The comments explain that synchronous communication has been replaced by implicit asynchronous communication and that failures are detected magically rather than via timeouts; because broadcast is modeled as a sequence of individual sends that can be interrupted by failure, the protocol is non-terminating and the usual termination property AC5 does not hold. The specification defines typed initial states, participant and coordinator actions, a next-state relation with weak fairness on non-death progress actions, and then states safety, liveness, stronger auxiliary properties, and explicitly invalid properties for the protocol.

993.specification: This module provides Apalache type annotations for another specification, ACP_SB, by declaring typed constants and variables and then instantiating the underlying module. The comments explain that the purpose is to keep the original specification free of tool-specific annotations while supplying concrete typing information for participants, participant state, coordinator state, and several tag constants such as yes, no, commit, and abort. The file itself does not define the protocol behavior, actions, or temporal properties; instead, it introduces the typed interface and a concrete set value for participants used by configuration.

994.specification: This module contains TLAPS proofs for two safety theorems from AllocatorImplementation.tla: that the system's Specification implies both the TypeInvariant and ResourceMutex properties. The TypeInvariant here combines the SchedulingAllocator's TypeInvariant (via the Sched! instance) with additional client-side variables, ensuring type correctness of the allocator state. The ResourceMutex property asserts that the holding sets of any two clients are disjoint unless the clients are the same, capturing client-side mutual exclusion. The proofs rely on an internal Invariant that combines the Sched-level AllocatorInvariant with a consistency invariant relating alloc, holding, and in-transit messages. The module includes detailed proofs for TypeInvariant and sketches for ResourceMutex, using well-founded induction and properties of permutation sequences over finite sets.

995.specification: This specification models a resource allocator that manages a finite set of resources for a set of clients, with explicit communication between clients and the allocator through a network of in-transit messages. Clients can issue requests only when they have no pending requests and hold no resources, allocations may satisfy requests only partially, and clients may return held resources even before their full request has been satisfied. The spec combines allocator state imported through an instance of a scheduling allocator with client-local state and message passing, and it verifies type correctness, a lower-level invariant relating allocator and client views, mutual exclusion of held resources, liveness of returns and eventual acquisition, and a recurring satisfaction property under weak fairness assumptions.

996.specification: This module states a refinement relationship between two allocator specifications. It extends SchedulingAllocator, instantiates SimpleAllocator as Simple, defines SimpleAllocator as Simple!SimpleAllocator, and asserts the theorem Allocator => SimpleAllocator.

997.specification: This module provides TLAPS proofs for the safety properties of the SchedulingAllocator specification. It proves that the Allocator specification implies the invariants TypeInvariant and ResourceMutex, ensuring type correctness and mutual exclusion of resources. The proofs rely on properties of sequences, finite sets, and permutation sequences, and use well-founded induction for reasoning about recursive definitions. The module also includes auxiliary lemmas about sequence operations and the structure of permutation sequences, and leaves the proof of AllocatorInvariant as future work due to its complexity.

998.specification: This module specifies a resource allocator for a finite set of clients and resources. Clients issue resource requests only when they have no outstanding unsatisfied request and currently hold no resources; requests may be partially satisfied, resources may be returned early, and a schedule sequence constrains which client requests may be served before others. The specification includes weak fairness assumptions requiring clients to return resources once fully satisfied, requiring allocations to eventually happen when enabled, and requiring scheduling to eventually occur; it states and checks type, mutual exclusion, allocator invariants, and several liveness properties such as eventual return, eventual obtainment of requested resources, and infinitely often satisfied requests.

999.specification: This module contains TLAPS proofs for two safety properties of the SimpleAllocator specification: that SimpleAllocator implies the invariants TypeInvariant and ResourceMutex. TypeInvariant is shown to be directly inductive, while ResourceMutex requires the combined invariant Inv (TypeInvariant and ResourceMutex) and an argument about the disjointness of allocated resources. The proofs are fully written in hierarchical style, with detailed reasoning about each action (Request, Allocate, Return) and the preservation of invariants. The module does not define the allocator algorithm itself, but proves properties about it using definitions and actions from the imported SimpleAllocator module.

1000.specification: This module specifies a simple resource allocator for a finite set of resources and a set of clients. Clients issue requests only when they currently hold no resources and have no outstanding unsatisfied request; requests may then be partially fulfilled over time, and clients may return held resources even before a request is completely satisfied. The specification defines two temporal system specifications with different fairness assumptions, and proves safety and liveness properties such as type correctness, mutual exclusion of resource ownership, eventual return, eventual obtainment, and infinitely often having no unsatisfied requests; it also includes a symmetry expression and a concrete counterexample value structure.

1001.specification: This module is a lightweight wrapper around another specification, intended to provide Apalache type annotations for a barrier specification instantiated from the module Barrier. It declares a constant N and a variable pc, and locally redefines the tuple vars as << pc >> in order to disambiguate the type of the 1-tuple used by the instantiated specification. The file itself contains no transition relation, temporal specification, or proof obligations; its main design purpose is to attach tool-specific typing information while leaving the original Barrier module unchanged.

1002.specification: This module specifies a simple reusable barrier synchronization protocol for N processes. Each process starts in control state "b0" and may individually move to "b1"; once all processes are in "b1", the barrier resets all processes back to "b0" simultaneously. The specification defines the initial state, the next-state relation, a type correctness condition for the program counter function, and a temporal barrier property stating that a process cannot leave the barrier while some other process has not yet entered it.

1003.specification: This module specifies and proves properties of a reusable barrier synchronization algorithm for N concurrent processes using two gates and a lock. The PlusCal algorithm models a two-chamber barrier in which processes first accumulate in a first waiting chamber, then pass through a second waiting chamber, preventing any process from re-entering the barrier too early and overtaking others. The translated TLA+ specification defines the operational steps a0 through a12, proves type correctness, mutual exclusion in the lock-protected critical section, several barrier invariants and a flush invariant, and finally proves that the detailed barrier implementation refines an abstract instantiated Barrier specification through a translated program counter view.

1004.specification: This TLA+ specification models a parameterized version of the one-round asynchronous reliable broadcast algorithm with Byzantine faults, as described in Srikanth and Toueg (1987). The model captures the behavior of correct and faulty processes, the sending and receiving of ECHO messages, and the acceptance of messages under Byzantine conditions. The specification is parameterized by the number of processes (N), the threshold for Byzantine faults (T), and the number of faulty processes (F), and it encodes both safety (unforgeability) and liveness (eventual acceptance) properties. Notably, the model supports both model checking (with TLC) and deductive verification (with TLAPS), and includes a full TLAPS proof of the unforgeability property, which asserts that if no correct process broadcasts a message, then no correct process ever accepts it. The design uses variables for the sets of correct and faulty processes to allow exploration of all possible assignments, and models the control state and message sets explicitly. The specification includes detailed invariants, fairness conditions, and inductive invariants to support both model checking and proof.

1005.specification: This module is a thin wrapper that supplies Apalache type annotations for another specification, `bcastFolklore`, via an `INSTANCE` declaration. It declares constants and variables with structured comments indicating intended integer, string, set, and function types, but it does not define any behavior, actions, temporal specification, or proof obligations of its own. The file therefore models no standalone algorithm directly; instead, it provides typed declarations intended to be used together with the instantiated module while keeping the original specification free of tool-specific annotations.

1006.specification: This TLA+ specification models the reliable broadcast algorithm by message diffusion, as described in Chandra and Toueg's 1996 paper on unreliable failure detectors. The model is parameterized by the number of processes (N), a threshold T, and the maximum number of allowed crashes F. It explicitly encodes process states, message sending and receiving, and crashed processes, and models only ECHO messages. The system allows processes to crash up to F times, and includes both the standard and a 'no broadcast' initialization. The specification checks type correctness, safety (unforgeability), and liveness properties, including that if a correct process broadcasts, all correct processes eventually accept, and that messages sent by correct processes are eventually received by all correct processes. Weak fairness is added to ensure liveness, and the model is designed for parameterized verification of fault-tolerant distributed algorithms under crash failures.

1007.specification: This module is an Apalache typing wrapper around another specification, bosco, rather than a standalone algorithm specification. It declares typed constants and variables and then instantiates the bosco module so that the original specification can remain free of tool-specific annotations. This file itself does not define the algorithm steps, temporal properties, or fault model; it only contributes type-annotated declarations and an INSTANCE of the underlying bosco module.

1008.specification: This specification models the BOSCO one-step Byzantine asynchronous consensus algorithm for a fixed set of processes, split into correct and faulty processes. Correct processes propose 0 or 1, broadcast ECHO messages, receive sets of messages that may also include Byzantine messages from faulty processes, and then either decide immediately or move to an underlying consensus with a chosen value. The spec assumes numeric constraints on N, T, and F, defines safety-oriented lemmas about incompatible decisions and underlying-consensus outcomes, includes a basic temporal specification Spec with Init and stuttering-enabled Next, and states two always-properties about executions starting from unanimous initial proposals.

1009.specification: This specification models a buffered random-access file implementation together with an abstract RandomAccessFile refinement target and shared array/file utilities. The main module specifies the buffered object's internal fields, the effects of seek, read, write, flush, and setLength, and a collection of internal invariants about how the in-memory buffer relates to the logical and on-disk file contents. It verifies both safety-style invariants and refinement properties: the whole behavior refines an abstract RandomAccessFile spec, and each concrete operation refines its abstract counterpart. The model is single-threaded and does not use an explicit fault model; instead, underspecified file contents are represented using an ArbitrarySymbol value to keep the model checkable. The file also includes a TLC configuration section selecting constants, symmetry, aliasing, invariants, and properties for model checking.

1010.specification: This specification models a B-tree-based key-value store supporting get, insert, and update requests over a bounded set of keys, values, and nodes. The state explicitly represents tree structure using node-local key sets, child pointers, last-child pointers, leaf flags, stored values, and a small request/response control interface with operational states for searching, adding, and splitting nodes. It includes a refinement mapping to an abstract kvstore specification, a type invariant and several structural invariants, and a temporal specification with weak fairness for get requests; there is no fault model, and comments note that deletes are not implemented.

1011.specification: This specification models a simple key-value store with four operations: get, insert, update, and delete. The store maps keys to either a value in Vals or the distinguished marker MISSING, and requests/responses are modeled with explicit state variables for the current operation, arguments, return value, and whether the system is ready or working. The spec defines type correctness, initialization, request and response actions for each operation, and a temporal specification requiring initialization, all steps to satisfy Next up to stuttering, and weak fairness for delete requests over op.

1012.specification: This module specifies voucher cancellation between a Voucher Transaction Provider (VTP), voucher holders, and voucher issuers using a simplified Two-Phase Commit protocol. The model represents messages as elements of a growing set, lets holders and issuers spontaneously prepare or abort, and lets the VTP either cancel once all parties are prepared or spontaneously abort the transaction. The specification checks a type-correctness invariant and a consistency invariant stating that a holder and an issuer never end in conflicting cancelled/aborted decisions, and it also states that this protocol specification implements an imported voucher life cycle specification.

1013.specification: This module specifies the issuance of vouchers between voucher issuers and voucher holders, coordinated by a voucher transaction provider using a simplified Two-Phase Commit style protocol. The model represents communication with a monotonically growing set of messages, omits explicit Prepare messages from the coordinator, and also omits explicit abort messages from holders and issuers, instead allowing the coordinator to abort spontaneously. It verifies type correctness and a consistency invariant stating that a holder and an issuer do not reach conflicting outcomes, and it also states that the protocol-level specification implements an imported voucher life cycle specification.

1014.specification: This module provides a TLAPS proof for the VoucherLifeCycle specification, specifically proving that the temporal property VSpec implies that the invariants VTypeOK and VConsistent always hold. The proof demonstrates that these two invariants together form an inductive invariant for the system. The proof is structured hierarchically and references the underlying system's initialization and next-state actions, but does not introduce new algorithmic behavior or fault models.

1015.specification: This specification models the life cycle of vouchers, based on RFC 3506, with the tuple component decoupled. Each voucher begins in a newly introduced "phantom" state before issuance, may become "valid", and can then either be redeemed or cancelled; transfer is allowed as a stuttering action while the voucher remains valid. The spec defines type correctness, initialization, a next-state relation over voucher actions, a consistency invariant relating voucher state to life-cycle machine state, and a temporal specification asserting behavior over all steps. It proves that under the specification, the conjunction of type correctness and consistency is always preserved.

1016.specification: This module specifies a voucher redemption protocol between voucher holders and voucher collectors coordinated by a voucher transaction provider using a simplified Two-Phase Commit style protocol. The model tracks voucher state, voucher life-cycle state, participant states, a set of received Prepared acknowledgments, and a global set of messages that only grows; messages are never removed, so reception is modeled by message presence. The specification proves that the protocol preserves type correctness and consistency, meaning holders and collectors do not reach conflicting redeemed versus aborted outcomes, and it also proves that the protocol implements an imported voucher life-cycle specification.

1017.specification: This module specifies a voucher transfer protocol modeled as a simplified Two-Phase Commit system. A Voucher Transaction Provider coordinates source holders and destination holders for transferring vouchers, with communication represented by a monotonically growing set of messages and with some protocol messages omitted for simplicity, as explained in the comments. The specification defines initialization, participant and coordinator actions, an invariant asserting type correctness and consistency between source and destination outcomes, and temporal properties stating that the overall protocol preserves those invariants and implements an imported voucher life-cycle specification.

1018.specification: This module specifies and proves properties of a Byzantine Paxos-style consensus algorithm called BPCon, an abstraction/generalization of Castro-Liskov Byzantine fault tolerance. The system models good acceptors, malicious fake acceptors, arbitrary leaders, message sets for phases 1a/1b/1c/2av/2b, and an auxiliary knowledge variable knowsSent that represents which 1b messages a good acceptor knows were sent. The specification includes the PlusCal algorithm, its generated TLA+ translation, a refinement mapping to an instantiated non-Byzantine Paxos module PConProof, an inductive invariant proof showing safety, and a theorem that the BPCon spec implements the abstract PCon spec under the refinement mapping.

1019.specification: This module specifies the consensus problem, which requires a set of processes to agree on a single value. The specification focuses on the core aspect of consensus: the selection of a single value from a set of possible values (Value), abstracting away the details of proposing and learning values. The safety property is modeled by allowing only a single state change in which the variable 'chosen' transitions from the empty set to a singleton set containing a value from Value, or remains unchanged. The module defines both safety (at most one value is chosen) and liveness (eventually some value is chosen, under fairness and non-emptiness assumptions) properties, and includes TLAPS proofs of invariance and liveness. Notably, the specification is minimal, with only one variable and a trivial next-state relation, and uses both temporal and fairness properties.

1020.specification: This module specifies and proves properties of a variant of Paxos consensus in which leaders may send phase 1c messages to assert that values are safe at a ballot before sending phase 2a proposals. The system models message-passing among ballot-indexed leaders and acceptors using a history variable msgs together with per-acceptor state maxBal, maxVBal, and maxVVal, and it refines an instantiated voting specification from module VoteProof. The file contains a PlusCal algorithm and its translated TLA+ form, proves equivalence between the translated Next relation and a manually structured TLA+ next-state relation, states invariants used for refinement and safety, and states a liveness theorem under fairness assumptions; the fault model is omission faults, represented by enabled actions and message receipts that may simply never occur.

1021.specification: This module specifies and proves properties of a voting protocol related to consensus, using acceptors, ballots, and quorums. It models acceptors maintaining a set of votes and a maximum ballot seen, defines a recursive safety predicate SafeAt, and proves state invariants ensuring vote consistency and safety. The file also contains TLAPS proofs showing inductive invariance, uniqueness of chosen values, refinement toward an instantiated Consensus specification, and a liveness assumption requiring weak fairness for some ballot actions while ruling out higher-ballot actions forever.

1022.specification: This module is an Apalache-oriented wrapper for the c1cs specification, providing type annotations and a typed witness for the tuple of state variables. It declares constants, variables, a vars tuple, instantiates the separate module c1cs, and defines concrete values for the otherwise uninterpreted VALUE constants.

1023.specification: This specification models the one-communication-step consensus algorithm with crash faults from the cited paper, focusing only on the algorithm itself and not the underlying consensus mechanism. Processes can propose values, receive broadcast messages, crash subject to a bound, decide based on thresholds over received proposed messages, and relay decision messages. The spec defines the transition system, a weak fairness condition for message receipt and progress actions, and asserts safety and liveness-style properties such as type correctness, validity, agreement, weak agreement, termination, and a stronger inductive strengthening predicate.

1024.specification: This specification models a crash-prone conditional consensus protocol in which processes exchange two phases of broadcast messages and use the maximal proposed value to drive decisions. The fault model is crash failures: up to F processes may crash, and crashed processes stop taking protocol steps. The spec defines initialization, message reception, both broadcast phases, local decision steps, and a deterministic fallback choose step, and it verifies typing, validity, agreement, unconditional termination as a temporal property, and a stronger conditional termination result under Condition1.

1025.specification: This module is a thin wrapper that adds Apalache type annotations to the original cf1s_folklore specification via an INSTANCE declaration. It declares integer constants and state variables corresponding to message counts, faulty-process counts, per-process program counters, and received-message counters. This file itself contains no top-level operator definitions, actions, assumptions, temporal formulas, or proofs.

1026.specification: This module specifies a one-step Byzantine consensus protocol, modeling only the core one-communication-step algorithm rather than the full underlying consensus procedure. It tracks how correct and faulty processes propose values, how messages are received, how processes decide or remain undecided, and how Byzantine faults can corrupt participating processes up to a bound F under the assumption N > 3 * T and T >= F >= 0. The specification defines both safety-style properties about decisions when all processes initially propose the same value and a liveness-oriented specification with weak fairness for non-faulty operational steps.

1027.specification: This module provides Apalache-oriented type annotations and concrete helper definitions for a Chang-Roberts leader election specification, while importing the main behavior from an instantiated module rather than redefining it here. It declares constants for the ring size and identifier sequence, variables for messages, program counters, initiator flags, and process state, and gives concrete top-level definitions for NVal and IdVal. The file itself contains no transition relation, temporal specification, fairness condition, or proof; its notable design choice is to keep tool-specific typing and concrete values in a wrapper module while leaving the original ChangRoberts specification separate.

1028.specification: This module specifies the Chang-Roberts leader election algorithm on a unidirectional ring of N nodes, where each node has a unique natural-number identity given by the sequence Id. The embedded comments explain that any subset of nodes may initiate the algorithm, and the node with the smallest identity is intended to be elected leader. The specification includes a PlusCal algorithm and its TLA+ translation, defines type correctness and a safety correctness condition about the winner and losing nodes, and states a liveness property that if some candidate exists then eventually some node wins. The temporal specification uses weak fairness for every process action and allows infinite stuttering through a Terminating action to avoid deadlock on termination.

1029.specification: This module is a minimal model-checking wrapper around another specification, likely the Chang-Roberts leader election algorithm, as indicated by the INSTANCE declaration. It introduces a single constant N and declares the variables msgs, pc, initiator, and state. The only explicit semantic constraint in this file is the assumption that N is a natural number, and it defines an identifier function Id mapping each process index in 1 .. N to itself.

1030.specification: This module is a test harness for BlockDag operators using small concrete directed acyclic graphs. It defines a tiny node set, round range, and round leader function, instantiates the BlockDag module with those concrete parameters, and then states a sequence of ASSUME-based test assertions about derived operators such as Node, Round, LeaderVertex, OrderSet, PreviousLeader, and Linearize. The specification is not a transition-system model with variables or temporal behavior; instead, it is a collection of concrete structural checks over finite sets, sequences, tuples, and a sample DAG.

1031.specification: This module defines helper notions on directed acyclic graphs for DAG-based consensus protocols, focusing on vertices that are pairs of a network node and a round. It defines leader vertices, a deterministic-but-arbitrary ordering of set elements, a way to find the previous leader in a DAG, and a recursive linearization procedure that turns a DAG into a sequence. The specification is not itself a full transition-system protocol model with variables and actions; instead it provides structural functions and predicates intended to support safety and liveness reasoning about DAG-based consensus, assuming a genesis vertex and that DAG paths terminate at genesis.

1032.specification: This module defines a directed graph abstraction represented as a pair consisting of a set of vertices and a set of edges. It provides operators to project the vertex and edge components, check whether a value is a well-formed digraph, compute the children of a vertex, compute the descendants reachable from a set of vertices using a recursive definition, and construct the reachable subgraph induced by a starting set of vertices. The module contains no variables, actions, temporal specification, fairness conditions, PlusCal algorithm, or proofs; it is a purely structural and recursive helper module for reasoning about directed graphs.

1033.specification: This module gives a high-level TLA+ specification of the Sailfish and Sailfish++ consensus algorithms, modeling a DAG-based protocol with correct and Byzantine nodes. The comments explain that Byzantine behavior is constrained because vertices are disseminated with reliable broadcast, so Byzantine nodes cannot equivocate and can only create protocol-conforming vertices subject to quorum checks. The specification defines initialization, the next-state relation for correct and Byzantine nodes, a basic type invariant, an agreement safety property over delivered logs, and a liveness property stating that after GST, leaders of synchronous rounds are eventually reflected in correct nodes' logs.

1034.specification: This module models a small bounded configuration of the Sailfish protocol with three nodes, one of which is Byzantine. The file defines concrete node sets, quorum and blocking-set predicates, a leader schedule, a global stabilization time constant, and a state constraint that bounds the explored rounds for non-faulty nodes to control state-space explosion. It introduces a terminating variant of the behavior specification and several deliberately false temporal/state predicates intended to help TLC produce interesting counterexample executions, including conditions about all correct nodes finishing and about committed log entries.

1035.specification: This specification models a particular configuration of the Sailfish protocol with four nodes, one of which is Byzantine. The comments state that any set of three nodes is treated as a quorum and any set of two nodes is treated as a blocking set, and the module defines node sets, a round range, quorum and blocking predicates, a fixed leader schedule, and a GST value. It declares protocol state variables and then defines a state constraint, a termination predicate, a terminating action that leaves the state unchanged, and a temporal specification that allows either normal protocol steps through Next or stuttering termination steps.

1036.specification: This module defines a small collection of utility operators for use by other specifications. It provides a generic reduction operator over an integer interval, simple arithmetic aggregation, sequence membership and removal helpers, a function range constructor, and a predicate for detecting whether a function induces a simple cycle over a finite set. The module is purely definitional: it declares no variables, no transition actions, and no temporal specification or fault model.

1037.specification: This module specifies an age-aware message channel in which messages are wrapped into boxes that carry both the original message content and an integer-valued transit age. The state tracks the set of boxed messages currently in transit and the set of messages delivered in the current transition, with actions for picking up new messages, delivering a nondeterministically chosen subset addressed to a given receiver, and advancing the age of all in-transit boxes. The specification includes initialization and a type invariant, but it does not define a full temporal specification such as Spec, fairness, or liveness properties; it focuses on the state representation and transition-level behavior of the channel.

1038.specification: This module specifies an eventually perfect failure detector in a partially synchronous distributed system. Each process maintains a local clock, a suspicion set, timeout values for other processes, and counters for how long it has been since it last heard from them; processes periodically send "alive" messages, receive incoming messages supplied by the environment, and periodically predict failures based on timeout expiration. The specification models adaptive timeouts by increasing a timeout when a previously suspected process is heard from again, and it includes a type invariant but no full temporal specification such as Spec, fairness, or liveness properties.

1039.specification: This module specifies an environment controller for an eventually perfect failure detector in a partially synchronous distributed system with crash faults. It composes process behavior and communication behavior via two instantiated modules, models message transit with ages, tracks local process clocks and pauses, and constrains executions using partial synchrony assumptions on message delay and relative process speeds. The specification verifies type correctness and temporal properties corresponding to Strong Completeness and Eventually Strong Accuracy, and includes a TLC state constraint used for bounded model exploration.

1040.specification: This specification models Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm, as described in his 1965 CACM paper. The algorithm ensures mutual exclusion among a set of processes (Proc), each of which cycles through non-critical and critical sections, using shared variables b, c, and k. The PlusCal translation is provided, and the TLA+ translation defines the system's state, actions, and temporal properties. The model checks mutual exclusion, deadlock freedom (under weak fairness), and discusses starvation freedom, with explicit invariants and liveness properties. The design allows for arbitrary process names and includes detailed commentary on the translation and fairness requirements.

1041.specification: This module is a TLC model wrapper for the DijkstraMutex specification rather than a standalone algorithm definition. It declares three model values p1, p2, and p3, defines a constant set containing those values for use as Proc in the model, and maps the model checking configuration to imported top-level operators from the extended module: LSpec as the behavior specification, MutualExclusion as an invariant, and DeadlockFreedom as a temporal property. The file itself contains no state variables, actions, fairness clauses, or proofs; it serves to instantiate and expose model-checking targets for the underlying mutex specification.

1042.specification: This specification models Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm for an arbitrary set of processes Proc, using a PlusCal algorithm and its generated TLA+ translation. The system uses shared variables b, c, and k together with per-process control state pc and a temporary local variable temp to represent each process progressing through entry protocol, critical section, and non-critical section. The specification includes the initial condition, next-state relation, and a fairness-based temporal specification Spec, and it defines safety and liveness properties including MutualExclusion, DeadlockFree, StarvationFree, and a stronger DeadlockFreedom property under an alternative liveness specification LSpec.

1043.specification: This module is a TLC model wrapper for the DijkstraMutex specification. It introduces four model-value constants p1, p2, p3, and p4, defines the process set Proc as the explicit set {p1, p2, p3, p4}, and maps the model behavior to the imported Spec operator and the model invariant to the imported MutualExclusion operator from the extended module. The file itself does not define the mutex algorithm, actions, or temporal properties internally; it only provides model-specific constants and aliases for checking the imported specification and invariant.

1044.specification: This module specifies Dijkstra's first published mutual exclusion algorithm, presented as a PlusCal algorithm together with its generated TLA+ translation. It models an arbitrary set Proc of processes that compete to enter a critical section using shared boolean arrays b and c and a shared process-valued variable k, with weak fairness assumptions for process steps in the main specification. The file defines the initial condition, per-control-location actions, the overall next-state relation and specification, and then states safety and liveness properties including mutual exclusion, deadlock freedom, starvation freedom, and a stronger deadlock-freedom property under a modified fairness interpretation.

1045.specification: This module specifies a disk-based variant of Synod/Paxos in which processes interact through persistent disks and maintain local phase, block, and read/write bookkeeping state. The model assumes each process has a disjoint positive ballot set, a distinguished set of disks with a majority predicate, and requires that any two disk majorities intersect. The specification defines initialization, phase-0 recovery reads, phase-1 and phase-2 writes and reads, ballot restarts, and failures, then verifies that the overall behavior refinement-style implies the imported SynodSpec theorem target.

1046.specification: This module augments the DiskSynod specification with additional history variables and inductive invariants for a disk-based Synod/Paxos-style consensus protocol. It introduces `allInput` to track every input value ever seen and `chosen` to record the first non-default output produced by any process, then states a series of higher-level invariants relating ballots, disk blocks, reads, majority sets, and the chosen value. The file does not define a full temporal specification of its own, but instead builds on the imported `Init` and `Next` actions from `DiskSynod` and adds safety-oriented predicates that characterize correctness of the protocol state.

1047.specification: This module is a small model-checking helper module for the HDiskSynod specification. It defines a concrete ballot-allocation operator that maps each process p to a contiguous range of ballot numbers of size BallotCountPerProcess, starting at p * BallotCountPerProcess. It also defines a concrete majority predicate stating that a set s is a majority exactly when Cardinality(s) * 2 > N; the module itself contains no temporal specification, actions, or proofs.

1048.specification: This specification models a simple Synod-style consensus abstraction over a set of processes 1..N, where each process has an input from Inputs and eventually may produce an output. The top-level module introduces an inner module that carries the actual state machine: it initializes each process output to a distinguished non-input value, tracks the set of all current inputs, and allows either a choice step that copies a selected value into an output or a failure-like step that changes a process input. The overall specification hides the internal variables chosen and allInput existentially, and it checks the temporal behavior of the inner system via the invariant-style initialization plus a boxed next-state relation without explicit fairness conditions.

1049.specification: This module specifies the Echo algorithm for constructing a spanning tree in an undirected connected graph starting from a single initiator. The graph is modeled by a set of nodes and a Boolean neighborhood relation R, with assumptions that R is irreflexive, symmetric, and connected; communication is modeled by per-node inbox sets containing message records. The PlusCal algorithm is included together with its TLA+ translation, and the specification verifies safety-style properties such as type correctness, absence of a parent for the initiator, parent-neighbor consistency, parent-child consistency, and ancestor properties at termination, as well as a termination temporal property stating that all processes eventually reach Done.

1050.specification: This module provides a concrete model-checking instantiation for an echo-style protocol specified in another module. It defines a tiny three-node graph, chooses an initiator nondeterministically from those nodes, and gives two concrete graph descriptions: one graph as a function over node pairs and one graph chosen to satisfy connectivity, symmetry, and irreflexivity assumptions. The module also defines a test specification that prints the relation at startup and then runs the imported specification, plus a simple view and postcondition using TLC-specific operators.

1051.specification: This module defines basic relational properties and operations for relations represented as binary Boolean functions over a set S. It provides predicates to check if a relation is reflexive, irreflexive, symmetric, asymmetric, transitive, and connected over a set. It also defines operators to compute the transitive closure and reflexive transitive closure of a relation, using recursive LET-bound operators and function constructors. The module is intended as a reusable library for reasoning about relations, and does not specify a particular algorithm or system, nor does it include temporal properties or proofs.

1052.specification: This module is a thin wrapper around another specification, intended to provide Apalache type annotations for the TokenRing specification while keeping the original module free of tool-specific annotations. It declares integer constants N and M, an integer-valued variable c typed as a function from Int to Int, and defines vars as the tuple << c >>. The module itself does not define an algorithm, transition relation, or temporal properties; instead, it instantiates the TokenRing module without explicit substitutions.

1053.specification: This module augments a token ring specification with simulation-oriented statistics collection and CSV logging. It assumes TLC is run in generate mode, initializes a CSV file header if the file is empty, and defines a state constraint-like operator that triggers when the underlying TokenRing model reaches stabilization, identified here by the predicate UniqueToken. Upon stabilization it writes the current TLC level to a CSV file, periodically invokes an external R script every 250 traces, and then returns FALSE so TLC continues simulation rather than terminating on stabilization.

1054.specification: This specification models Dijkstra's classical self-stabilizing token ring algorithm from EWD426. The system consists of N nodes arranged in a ring, each storing a counter value in a bounded domain 0..M-1; node 0 can create a new token by incrementing relative to the last node, while every other node passes the token by copying its predecessor when their values differ. The spec assumes at least one node and a nonempty value domain, together with the condition N <= M + 1, and it verifies a stabilization property stating that eventually the system reaches and stays in a state with a unique token.

1055.specification: This module specifies the Dijkstra-Scholten distributed termination detection algorithm for a diffusing computation initiated by a distinguished root node. The system maintains a dynamic spanning tree of active nodes, with nodes sending base messages, receiving acknowledgments, detaching from the tree when inactive and childless, and the initiator declaring termination when it becomes inactive and has no remaining children. The specification includes a PlusCal algorithm and its TLA+ translation, models bounded message counts for state-space exploration, assumes a finite node set with an initiator in that set, and verifies both a safety property that termination implies quiescence and a liveness property that quiescence leads to eventual termination under weak fairness of each process action.

1056.specification: This module defines an animation and visualization layer for the EWD687a specification, rendering states of a process network as SVG graphics and exporting frames to files. It models graph layout, node and edge rendering, overlay information such as active and neutral processes, message and acknowledgment counts, and a legend describing the current TLC action and level. It also adds simulation-oriented predicates such as an interesting behavior condition and a constraint disallowing superfluous idle stuttering steps, while relying on the underlying EWD687a module for the actual protocol state and dynamics.

1057.specification: This module provides TLAPS proofs for the theorems stated in EWD687a.tla, which models a distributed termination detection algorithm based on Dijkstra's EWD687. The system involves processes communicating over edges, with counters tracking sent, received, acknowledged, and in-flight messages. The proofs establish inductive invariants for counter consistency, tree structure, and acyclicity, and relate these to properties such as global termination and the existence of a spanning tree rooted at the leader. The module also interfaces with the community Graphs module to formalize tree properties, and includes detailed hierarchical proofs for safety properties, while some liveness and path-construction arguments are left as future work or omitted.
